#723. China’s Film Industry Arrives at AFM on a Domestic High

Revenue still trails last year’s 'Ne Zha 2'-fueled peak, but homegrown hits are driving the 2026 box office and the industry is courting partners abroad.

Chinese filmmaker Wen Muye keeps taking what look on paper like challenging subjects and turning them into box office gold.

It began with his 2018 debut, Dying to Survive, about a man (Xu Zheng) who makes a fortune smuggling cancer drugs into China. The film took in more than $450 million, and Wen was hailed as an exciting new voice in Chinese cinema. He blended so much humanity and humor into the story that, by the time the credits rolled, the film had become the tale of a man who went looking for cash but found his soul.

When news of Wen’s latest venture broke, Chinese media initially struggled with what they’d heard of Once Upon a Time in the Middle East: the fact that it would be set in the war-torn Middle East, inside a Chinese restaurant, and would star one of the country’s most beloved comedians in Shen Teng (Pegasus) led to some head scratching. Related Stories Movies Can Constantin Survive Its Own Parent Company? Movies Magnolia Pictures Takes French Animated Gay Comedy 'Jim Queen' for U.S.

But, again, Wen has worked his magic. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East became a $360 million-odd hit at home, thanks in no small part to the filmmaker’s talent for mixing genres, with warm humor to be found along with moments of dramatic devastation, and what might well be a career-defining turn from Shen. Again, as with Wen’s first feature, it’s the tale of an everyman turned hero.

The director points to three key ingredients when he was writing the script and working on the ways in which he would present the movie to the world: Wen says he was looking to combine “entertainment value” with “social relevance” and “soulfulness.” To do that, he presents an assortment of relatable characters, drawn together through circumstance and held together by their shared humanity.

“Even if the audience does not usually think about big questions, after watching it, would they be willing to think about things like war and peace, hope and human relationships?” begins Wen. “These three levels go deeper and deeper. It is already not easy to achieve entertainment value. [But] if one can also enter social relevance and finally leave a longer spiritual memory, that is of course the state I hope for.”

Wen’s film has become one of the biggest success stories in the world’s second-largest film market, and it’s now the country’s official submission in the international Oscar category. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East is also down for one of four market screenings being hosted at AFM by the China Film Pavilion, an initiative staged under the guidance of China Film Administration, hosted by the China Film Co-production Corporation (CFCC) and back at the market for the fourth year in a row.

Those screenings reflect the recent move toward a more varied output from the Chinese film industry. Alongside the star vehicle that is Once Upon a Time in the Middle East comes the Lan Hongchun-directed box office smash Dear You ($300 million) — a gentle but sweeping family drama — as well as the animated hit Boonie Bears: The Hidden Protector, the 12th release in the blockbuster franchise that has taken in more than $1 billion in China alone. Rounding out the CFCC’s AFM slate is the documentary Daughter of the River, drawn from the memoirs of acclaimed author Hong Ying and tracing the lives of generations of women living in the southwestern city of Chongqing.

This year’s China Film Pavilion has showcased 70 film companies and institutions, among them the China Film Group Corporation, CMC Pictures, Lianray Pictures, China Film Archive, China Film Foundation and the Shanghai International Film Festival. As well as market screenings (held at MC Century City), the on-site AFM facility has been promoting more than 200 titles, among them the much-anticipated sci-fi epic The Wandering Earth 3 — a franchise that has so far collected roughly $1.3 billion — the Jiang Xuanyi-helmed actioner Brotherhood of Blades 3 and the animated fantasy hit All Wishes Come True!

Other initiatives this year include a mixer on Nov. 11 at which leading Chinese industry figures will discuss the state of their domestic scene while showcasing more films. There will also be a main-market, CFCC-hosted seminar titled “Beyond Co-Production: New Models for Financing, Creating, and Distributing Global Screen IP” that focuses on four issues: “how to combine financing, talent and production resources from different countries; how to incorporate global distribution and audience considerations from the project planning stage; how AI can reduce production costs while preserving creators’ unique styles; and how to carry out cross-cultural redevelopment of classic films and established IP.”

The session is moderated by Rance Pow, founder and CEO at Artisan Gateway — the Los Angeles-based consulting firm that offers analysis of the Chinese film industry — and features as panelists Apelles Entertainment founder Belle Avery; executive vp and head of corporate banking at East West Bank Bennett Pozil; founder and CEO at Leeding Media David Lee; senior global entertainment executive at U.S. China Co-Productions Randy Greenberg; and William Feng, who’s head of Greater China and vp at the Motion Picture Association Asia Pacific.

The aim, according to the CFCC, is to explore “new avenues for global cooperation” and to “facilitate international film transactions, solidify Sino-foreign cinematic partnerships and boost cultural appreciation within the global industry.”

The Chinese industry arrives for AFM boosted by a run of successful local hits in 2026 and some positive box office news. By the end of October, revenue had topped $4.7 billion, with more than 800 million admissions and roughly 122 million screenings, according to state-run media reports. Year-on-year, China is still down around 29 percent — with the caveat that 2025 was bumped by the freakish success of the animated hit Ne Zha 2, which took in a staggering $2.2 billion. But what seems to be driving optimism is the fact that 2026’s overall box office is mostly being driven by domestic releases.

By October’s end, eight of the country’s top 10 films for the year were local, led by the action-comedy Pegasus 3 ($656 million) and followed by Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.

Wen’s own explanation for his film’s success is more straightforward. He puts it down to the fact that, on so many levels, the characters and the conversations they have are so relatable.

“I have always been interested in the state of ordinary people in specific environments, because ordinary people are not making big choices every day,” says Wen. “Most of the time, they are dealing with very concrete things like eating, work, family, money and relationships. But when circumstances truly push them into a certain position, they may also do things they could not normally do. For me, this change is not about first writing a hero and then adding an ordinary person’s life to him. It is about starting from an ordinary person and seeing how far he can go under the pressure of reality.”

SpaceX is counting down to make history with the launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13, with liftoff scheduled for 5:45 p.m. EDT (2245 GMT) at Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land both Starship Ship and Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever full recovery of an orbital rocket and spacecraft, if successful.

Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which will also deliver 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.

Flight 15 livestream | SpaceX | Starship | Starship V3 explained

Happy Wednesday, Space Fans. We are now T-2 days away from SpaceX's planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 test mission, so I wanted to take a moment to give you a run down on what to expect.

Today, you can read my full guide to SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch here, which goes over what time and where to watch the launch online. Liftoff is on track for Friday, Nov. 13, at 4:45 p.m. CST, which is 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). But it ALSO (and this is new) includes what time to tune in a day later for the planned Starship upper stage (Ship) landing and catch by the metal "Chopstick" arms of its landing pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility in South Teas.

If you're wondering how the rocket's assembly is going, our Spaceflight Editor Mike Wall has this update on the Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy booster going through final catch tests yesterday. Flight 15 will mark the first time SpaceX will attempt to land and catch both the Super Heavy booster (which it has done several times) and the Ship from orbit.

If successful, it will be the first full recovery of an entire orbital rocket from space.

Hello, Space Fans, and welcome to our coverage of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight, the first ever to attempt twin landings of the Starship Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage.

SpaceX has officially set the launch date for Flight 15 for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EDT (2145 GMT). That puts launch just about 3 days away and Space.com will provide live coverage of the potentially historic flight, the first full recovery of an orbital rocket.

Space.com Spaceflight Writer Josh Dinner will be reporting live from near SpaceX's Starbase , Texas site for the launch, with myself (Tariq Malik), Spaceflight and Tech Editor Mike Wall and other team members tracking the flight remotely for you here. #721. NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary era of astronomical discovery to a close. The spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, ending a mission that lasted more than ten times longer than originally planned.

Launched in 2004, Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes designed to study some of the most powerful explosions in the universe. Its instruments could detect different types of light, allowing scientists to investigate energetic cosmic events that would be difficult to understand using a single telescope.

NASA's Swift Observatory Re-Enters Earth's Atmosphere

The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.

NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere. However, officials acknowledged that some components might have survived the intense heat of re-entry.

A Two-Year NASA Mission That Lasted Nearly 22 Years

Swift was originally developed to investigate gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily powerful flashes of high-energy radiation associated with some of the most extreme events in the cosmos. These bursts can occur when massive stars collapse or when certain compact objects, such as neutron stars, merge.

Although NASA initially planned for Swift to operate for just two years, the observatory continued making scientific contributions for more than two decades.

One of its most important capabilities was its ability to respond quickly to sudden cosmic events. When Swift detected an energetic outburst, it could rapidly redirect its telescopes toward the source and notify observatories around the world. This coordinated approach allowed astronomers to study brief astronomical phenomena before they faded from view.

Swift also observed multiple wavelengths of light, giving researchers different ways to examine the same event and better understand the physical processes behind it.

Over its remarkably long lifetime, Swift's scientific contributions expanded far beyond its original focus on gamma-ray bursts.

The observatory helped astronomers investigate active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars that produce powerful X-ray flares, and supernovae, the enormous explosions that mark the deaths of certain stars.

Its observations also extended much closer to home, including studies of comets and asteroids within our own solar system.

By combining rapid observations with the ability to detect different forms of radiation, Swift became a valuable tool for exploring both distant cosmic explosions and nearby objects. Its re-entry marks the end of a mission that greatly exceeded its planned lifespan and helped transform scientists' understanding of some of the universe's most energetic phenomena.

#720. Jessica Chastain to Star on Broadway in ‘Lost Lear’

Michael Urie and Corey Stoll will also star in the play at the Booth Theatre this spring.

Jessica Chastain has confirmed her return to Broadway in the new play Lost Lear.

The play, written and directed by Dan Colley, follows a former actress with dementia who imagines she’s back in rehearsal for King Lear. Corey Stoll will star as her estranged son, with Michael Urie starring as her nurse, stepping into various roles in the play.

Chastain returns to Broadway after starring in the 2023 Broadway revival of A Doll’s House. The Academy Award winner teased the return on the Today show last week, while promoting her new Netflix film Heartland.

The play is set to begin performances at the Booth Theatre on March 29, with an opening night on April 23. It comes to Broadway after premiering at Dublin Theatre Festival in 2022 and touring the U.S., U.K. and New Zealand. The play won the Scotsman Fringe First award at Edinburgh Festival Fringe in 2025.

“I never imagined, when we first made Lost Lear, that it would one day be on Broadway – and I’ve imagined some pretty wild things,” Colley said. “I’m so thrilled to have the opportunity to share this piece with New York audiences and to discover new facets of the work through collaborating with this remarkable company of artists.”

Urie, who stars as Brian in Apple TV+’s Shrinking, most recently appeared on Broadway in Oh, Mary! after a long list of Broadway credits including the 2024 revival of Once Upon a Mattress, Spamalot and the revival of Harvey Fierstein’s Torch Song.

Stoll, also known for his role as Peter on House Of Cards, among many onscreen appearances, returns to Broadway after being Tony nominated for his role in the 2024 revival of Appropriate.

Seaview, MarketStall and Mass Productions with Pam Hurst-Della Pietra & Stephen Della Pietra are producing. Additional casting will be announced at a later date.

#718. Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky

November 2026 is packed with celestial events worth watching, from brilliant meteors streaking across the sky to a striking encounter between Mars and Jupiter. NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is also approaching an extraordinary milestone, while a dazzling supermoon will close out the month.

Three meteor showers offer multiple opportunities to catch shooting stars, including occasional fireballs bright enough to stand out dramatically against the night sky. Meanwhile, two of the solar system's most recognizable planets will appear unusually close together just before sunrise.

As if that weren't enough, humanity's most distant spacecraft is reaching a point where radio signals from Earth take an entire day to arrive.

Here's what NASA recommends watching for in November.

Three Meteor Showers Could Light Up November's Sky

November gives skywatchers several chances to see meteors flash across the darkness. The first opportunities come from the Southern and Northern Taurids, two related meteor showers that reach their highest activity levels about a week apart.

The Southern Taurids peak around November 5, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12. Both showers get their names from the constellation Taurus, where their meteors appear to originate when viewed from Earth.

Neither shower is especially prolific. Even under excellent conditions, each typically produces only about five meteors per hour. However, the Taurids are known for occasionally producing impressive fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors that can make even a relatively quiet night of skywatching memorable.

The Leonids provide another opportunity later in the month. Their best viewing periods are expected during the early morning hours of November 17 and 18, particularly after the Moon has disappeared below the horizon. Under ideal conditions, observers could see approximately 15 meteors per hour, although actual counts will generally be lower.

For the best chance of spotting meteors, travel somewhere away from bright city lights. Allow your eyes roughly 30 minutes to become accustomed to the darkness, then watch a broad section of the sky rather than concentrating on one small area.

Mars and Jupiter Appear Almost Side by Side

Meteor showers aren't the only reason to get outside before dawn. On November 15 and 16, Mars and Jupiter will create an eye-catching pairing in the southeastern sky.

The two planets will appear separated by only about 1.2 degrees, slightly more than the apparent width of two full Moons placed next to each other.

Jupiter will be the brighter of the two, making it relatively easy to identify. Nearby, Mars will stand out with its characteristic reddish appearance.

No telescope or binoculars will be necessary to enjoy the sight. Both planets should be readily visible to the unaided eye under suitable viewing conditions.

Although they will appear remarkably close from Earth's perspective, Mars and Jupiter remain separated by enormous distances in space. Their apparent proximity is simply a result of their positions along our line of sight.

Watching the planets over several consecutive mornings will reveal another interesting feature of their motion. They will gradually appear to move closer together before their positions shift and they begin separating again.

Voyager 1 Reaches an Extraordinary Deep Space Milestone

While November offers plenty to observe in Earth's skies, something equally remarkable is happening far beyond the planets.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is reaching a historic distance of one light-day from Earth, becoming the first human-made object ever to travel that far from our planet.

A light-day is the distance light travels through space in 24 hours. Because radio signals move at the speed of light, a message transmitted from Earth will require an entire day to reach Voyager 1 at that distance.

If the spacecraft sends a response immediately, the return signal will take another 24 hours to arrive. That means even the fastest possible round-trip communication will require approximately 48 hours.

The milestone illustrates just how far Voyager 1 has traveled since leaving Earth and how challenging it has become to communicate with a spacecraft exploring such distant regions of space.

To get a sense of the spacecraft's current direction, look toward the constellation Ophiuchus, also known as the Serpent Bearer. Voyager 1 is traveling through space in that general direction, far beyond anything visible to the unaided eye.

NASA is marking the achievement on November 17 with its Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day activation, inviting people to celebrate this extraordinary accomplishment in space exploration.

November's Supermoon Begins a Three-Month Celestial Show

The final major skywatching highlight arrives on November 24, when a full supermoon will rise into the evening sky.

A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with a period when the Moon is relatively close to Earth in its orbit. Because the Moon follows a slightly elliptical path rather than a perfect circle, its distance from our planet changes throughout the month.

When a full Moon occurs near the closer portion of that orbit, it can appear somewhat larger and brighter than an average full Moon. Although the difference is real, it is often subtle enough that casual observers may not immediately notice it.

November's event is particularly noteworthy because it begins a sequence of three consecutive supermoons. Another will follow in December, with a third arriving in January.

For an especially memorable view, NASA recommends looking toward the eastern horizon around sunset on November 24, when the full Moon will be rising.

The Moon may seem unusually enormous when it first appears near the horizon. However, much of that dramatic impression comes from a familiar visual phenomenon called the Moon illusion.

This optical effect makes the Moon appear larger when it is close to the horizon than when it is high overhead, even though its actual apparent size changes very little. The illusion can occur during any full Moon, not just a supermoon.

With three meteor showers, a close planetary pairing, a historic Voyager 1 milestone, and the beginning of a supermoon series, November offers plenty of reasons to look up and explore the night sky.

#717. ‘One in a Million’ Filmmaker on the Ethical Dilemma He Faced and Learning to Let His Subject Find Her Own Way

Over a decade, co-directors Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes documented a young Syrian girl named Israa and her family's changing dynamics as refugees in Germany.

For One in a Million filmmakers Jack MacInnes and Itab Azzam, documenting the life of a Syrian refugee family for more than a decade meant confronting a complicated question: What’s the line between documenting the truth and protecting your subject?

That conundrum came to a head when a 14-year-old girl named Israa, whom the married documentarians had been following since the age of 11, when her parents decided to immigrate from Turkey to Germany, revealed that her father, Tarek, had hit her. The disclosure came as a shock, given the close relationship they initially witnessed between the pair. Related Stories SCAD Savannah Film Festival "It's All Cinema!" Directors of 2026's Top Docs on Taking Risks, Interacting With Subjects and the Huge Success of 'You Can See Everything' (Video) Movies 'You Can See Everything' Sweeps Critics Choice Documentary Awards

“In the first part of the film, he really is a heroic father,” MacInnes said during a Q&A following a screening of the documentary at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival on Oct. 29. “It just felt like this moment of the scales falling from our eyes,” he added of the revelation. “Have we been naive? What is happening here?”

When the filmmakers returned to their home base of London, they questioned whether they should continue with the project and ensured Israa had the proper resources available to her. Her mother, Nisreen, pleaded with the duo, saying, “‘Don’t tell anyone. We want to deal with this ourselves,’” MacInnes recalled.

“We were obviously worried,” he explained further. “But it turned out Nisreen did have the courage to act and to tend to and look after her children, which ended up becoming the story.”

When the documentary picks up two years later, Nisreen has left Tarek and is happily raising their four children alone, encouraging other women to leave an unhappy relationship despite the difficulty of being a single parent. “The fact that she emerges from the shadows and finds herself — finds her voice — is such a key part of the story,” MacInnes said. Tarek, on the other hand, is living alone in a refugee camp, unable to face the reality of his actions.

Israa’s status at the time is a bit more complicated: the then-16-year-old newly embracing her Muslim faith and wearing the hijab, as she declares her boyfriend, Mohammed, has helped her find freedom through her religion. It’s a development that initially surprised MacInnes and Azzam, particularly in light of her mother’s transformation, he admitted.

“The real exercise for the second half of the film [was] where we started to look at our own prejudices and our own views and started to think, the dreams we thought were her dreams, how much of that was our dreams for her?” he said.

“It’s one of the reasons, at the end of the film, I loved coming back to [Israa’s] dreams when she came into Germany. She wasn’t saying, ‘I want to be an astronaut; I want to go to university.’ She was saying, ‘I want a home, and I want a bed.’ And that’s when we came to realize that what she had lost was family; her family had fallen apart. She’d lost home, she’d lost stability, she’d lost love,” MacInnes said.

The filmmakers continued following the journey of Israa, now 21, through her marriage to Mohammed, their family’s first visit back to Syria following the fall of President Bashar al-Assad’s regime in 2024 and even Israa’s reconciliation with her father, who, near the end of the film, is finally able to own up to his abuse and is building a new relationship with his daughter as a grandfather to her and Mohammed’s son.

“I was talking to Israa yesterday, and she was saying what she’s found is love. And we thought, if she’s found peace and love in this life she’s chosen, then actually there’s a lot for us to learn from that,” said MacInnes. “We came to a place where we saw what she was getting from her Muslim faith, which was peace and faith, and it’s beautiful, I think.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Astronomers have solved the mystery of an extrasolar planet, or exoplanet, that "disappeared" after seven years of observations. New research suggests that the planet hasn't vanished at all, but has been dragged off its orbit by an unseen planet.

The exoplanet, designated TOI-2535 b, is located around 1,000 light-years away. TOI-2535 b was routinely observed with NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) space telescope for seven years between April 2019 and March 2026 as it completed its 8.25-Earth day orbit of its parent star. That's 10 times quicker than the orbit of Mercury around the sun and means this blisteringly hot planet is classed as a "hot Jupiter."

However, something strange happened started to happen as astronomers observed the distant world. The orbits of the planet weren't regular like those of other planets, with TOI-2535 b often arriving six hours early or six hours later than when astronomers expected. Then, in March this year, TESS was no longer spotting the characteristic drops in starlight that TOI-2535 b caused as it crossed, or "transited," the face of its parent star. It seemed to have vanished.

This team used TESS data to determine that TOI-2535 b is being pulled on by an unseen neighbor and is, in turn, pulling on that planet as well. This is causing the orbits of both worlds in the TOI-2535 system to "wobble." TOI-2535 b disappeared when that wobble tilted it out of alignment with its star.

"We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that's not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other's orbits. We know of a few systems that are like this," team member Samuel Yee of the University of California, Los Angeles, said in a statement. "This is the most extreme example we've seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly. The planet's orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching."

TOI-2535 b isn't expected to transit its parent star for at least 30 years, but the hidden neighbor tugging on it may cross the face of the star sooner than that.

In the meantime, scientists will attempt to decode what this extreme wobbling exoplanet system says about how it formed.

There is currently a lot of speculation about how hot Jupiter planets like TOI-2535 b form. That is because current routes of planet formation suggest planets like this would need to form around a great deal of ice. Obviously, ice isn't likely to be abundant as close to a star as TOI-2535 b is currently.

This means that hot Jupiters likely form far from their stars and then migrate inwards. There are two ways that this could happen. The planet could be excited into an elliptical orbit by violent events like a near-collision with another planetary object, and then interactions with the star pull the planet inwards.

Alternatively, the hot Jupiter may be pulled inwards along with the other planets while sitting in a flattened cloud of gas and dust around the infant star called a protoplanetary disk.

If this second, less turbulent route occurs to bring hot Jupiters close to their stars, then the resultant system should be very flat. In other words, there shouldn't be extreme tilts between the orbits of the planets in that system.

However, the tilt caused to TOI-2535 b by its unseen companion indicates that flattened systems can be twisted by more tilted orbits later in their existence. This makes the slower migration possible despite the orbital tilt.

"Because TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in," Yee said. "We may be seeing a formation channel that doesn’t happen very often but is very interesting."

The team's research was published on Monday (Nov. 9) in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.

#715. Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth

For nearly a century, scientists have considered the possibility that comets helped make life on Earth possible by delivering essential organic molecules from space. Now, new research suggests this long-standing explanation is extremely unlikely.

Comets are known to contain many of the chemical compounds associated with the origins of life. These substances, often called prebiotic molecules, can participate in the chemical reactions that eventually produce the complex ingredients needed for living organisms. For decades, researchers have proposed that comets striking the early Earth supplied a steady stream of these compounds.

However, a new study led by the University of Cambridge challenges that theory. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers found that comets generally approach Earth at speeds and angles that make it extremely difficult for delicate organic molecules to survive. Instead of delivering their chemical cargo intact, most would likely destroy it during their violent arrival.

The findings, published in Scientific Reports, suggest that successful delivery of life's building blocks by comets would have been an extraordinarily rare event. Interestingly, the researchers also found that Mars may have offered somewhat better conditions for receiving these molecules, although the likelihood remains very low.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get out of jail free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge's Institute of Astronomy. "It's kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it's highly unlikely."

Why Comets May Have Failed to Deliver Life's Building Blocks

The idea that comets could transport the ingredients for life received renewed attention in 2023, when Anslow and several colleagues explored how these icy objects might behave in planetary systems where worlds orbit relatively close together.

Their earlier research suggested that comets could potentially lose speed as they passed between neighboring planets. Through a series of gravitational encounters, a comet might effectively bounce from one planet to another, eventually traveling slowly enough to deliver organic molecules without destroying them.

The team wanted to determine whether a similar process could have occurred in our own Solar System, potentially explaining how essential chemicals reached the young Earth.

"We're learning more and more all the time about how our Solar System and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century," he said.

To investigate, the researchers combined several sophisticated modeling techniques. These included simulations of comet impacts, calculations of how comets interact with planetary atmospheres, and models tracing how comet populations formed and changed as the Solar System developed.

The results revealed a major obstacle. Although a comet might occasionally approach Earth under conditions favorable for preserving organic compounds, such encounters would have been exceptionally uncommon. Successful delivery could not be completely ruled out, but the simulations indicated that it was highly improbable.

A Critical Ingredient for Life Faces Nearly Impossible Odds

To better understand what happens to the molecules carried by comets, the team concentrated on hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a chemical commonly detected in comets throughout our Solar System.

Despite its reputation as a highly toxic substance, hydrogen cyanide is important in research on the origins of life. It contains carbon and nitrogen and can participate in reactions that produce more complex organic compounds, making it a potentially valuable ingredient in the chemistry that preceded living organisms.

The simulations showed that even when hydrogen cyanide managed to survive a comet's arrival, another major problem remained. The impact would need to deposit enough of the molecule in one location to support meaningful chemical reactions. Events capable of producing those useful concentrations were extraordinarily rare.

Timing created yet another difficulty. Comet impacts were much more common during Earth's earliest history, but their frequency declined sharply over the planet's first 500 million years. According to the researchers, there may have been only a handful of opportunities during that entire early period for comets to deliver hydrogen cyanide under favorable conditions.

Even a successful delivery would not necessarily have helped life develop. Hydrogen cyanide deposited on Earth's surface would likely have dispersed or become diluted relatively quickly, leaving little time for the chemical reactions associated with life's origins to get underway.

For the comet theory to work, several unlikely events would therefore have needed to occur together. A comet would have had to strike at just the right speed and angle, preserve its organic cargo, deposit enough material in a suitable location, and trigger important chemical processes before those molecules dispersed.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can't rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence - at best, a one-off fluke."

If Not Comets, Where Did Life's Ingredients Come From?

The findings raise a fundamental question about Earth's earliest history. If comets were unlikely to supply the chemical building blocks of life, what was responsible?

One possibility involves asteroids, which collided with the early Earth far more frequently than comets. The researchers suggest that asteroid impacts could have created conditions in which important prebiotic molecules formed through chemical reactions associated with those collisions.

Another explanation is that Earth produced these compounds on its own. Natural chemical processes operating on the young planet may have generated the ingredients necessary for increasingly complex chemistry, without requiring organic molecules to arrive from space.

These possibilities do not establish exactly how life began. Instead, they highlight alternative ways that the raw materials for life could have become available on Earth.

Why Mars May Have Had a Better Chance Than Earth

While the simulations cast serious doubt on cometary delivery to Earth, they also revealed an intriguing possibility involving Mars.

The Red Planet is smaller than Earth and currently has a much thinner atmosphere. These characteristics make it a potentially more favorable destination for cometary molecules, since incoming objects could be more likely to reach its surface without completely destroying their chemical cargo.

According to the researchers, Mars may therefore have been better positioned to receive prebiotic compounds during the Solar System's early development, when comet encounters were considerably more frequent.

However, the simulations do not demonstrate that such deliveries actually occurred. Even on Mars, the conditions required for a successful transfer of life's chemical ingredients appear difficult to achieve.

"This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn't happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn't happen on either planet."

What the Discovery Means for the Search for Alien Life

Beyond changing how scientists think about Earth's early chemistry, the findings could help guide the search for potentially habitable planets in other star systems.

Future space observatories may be able to investigate distant worlds in greater detail, searching for atmospheric clues that could indicate environments suitable for life. Among the proposed missions is the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a potential successor to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The researchers suggest that planetary systems where comets can move between closely spaced planets while gradually losing speed may deserve particular attention. In such environments, the unusual comet delivery mechanism explored in their earlier research could be more likely to operate.

Identifying these systems could help astronomers focus future observations on planets where essential organic molecules may have had a better chance of surviving their journey through space.

Although the new findings make comets an unlikely explanation for how life's building blocks reached Earth, they do not eliminate the possibility that cometary delivery played a role elsewhere. Understanding where these chemical transfers are possible could provide valuable clues as scientists continue investigating how life emerges across the universe.

The research received partial support from the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Centre for Life in the Universe, and the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), which is part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI).

#714. ‘VisionQuest’ Creator Terry Matalas Tells All About That Supersized Finale and Post-Credits Surprise

The former 'Picard' showrunner also pays tribute to the late Patrick Stewart in a spoiler-filled chat with THR about the final chapter of the WandaVision trilogy: "All endings need to touch on the beginning."

[This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the finale of VisionQuest, “Forever.”]

For showrunner Terry Matalas, VisionQuest was always going to be a Marvel show about fathers and sons.

When he was tapped a few years ago to redevelop the final chapter of the WandaVision trilogy — taking over from creator Jac Schaeffer, who reportedly stepped away from the project to focus on Agatha All Along, the second installment starring Kathryn Hahn — Matalas received just one clear directive from Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige. The new sequel series had to center on Paul Bettany’s synthezoid Vision and his superpowered son Tommy Maximoff — one of the twin boys he shared with Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen), the Scarlet Witch who ostensibly perished at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. Related Stories TV Streaming Ratings: 'From' Netflix Effects Its Way to Top of the Charts General News "You Shall Not Pass": Gandalf, Black Panther and Deadpool Take to the Streets of France

“We knew Tommy was going to be a part of it, and then I had to ask myself, ‘Who is Vision talking to? He doesn’t have Wanda in this show, and Tommy felt like something you want to get to,’” Matalas explains to The Hollywood Reporter. “So I immediately went to Vision’s father, and specifically Ultron [played by] James Spader. I was so enamored by that last scene in Avengers: Age of Ultron between the two of them and asked myself, ‘Well, what if that was the show?’”

Over the course of eight episodes, the newly resurrected “White Vision” — whose original memories had been locked away by the agency S.W.O.R.D. following his death in Avengers: Infinity War, only to have them unlocked by the Hex-created version of himself in the WandaVision finale before flying away — embarks on a deeply psychological journey of self-discovery. As he grapples with his fractured identity, Vision confronts a philosophical, mirror-image Ultron — his deeply toxic, cynical creator functioning as a dark father figure — and struggles to accept Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica), an orphaned teenager who is the super-powered reincarnation of his and Wanda’s son Tommy.

Though she was credited as an executive producer, Schaeffer was not creatively involved in VisionQuest, wanting to give Matalas and his writers’ room — most of whom had worked with him on Star Trek: Picard — “a blank canvas” to play with. “I called her briefly to thank her and just because I’m such a fan of what she did with WandaVision. I watched every episode of that twice when it came out and then would go on YouTube and dissect every single Easter egg,” Matalas says. “But she was very clear upfront that she didn’t want to share any creative [input].”

The VisionQuest finale, however, still pays tribute to WandaVision and Agatha in more ways than one. The series’ overarching puppet master — revealed to be “The Client,” Virgil Horton (also played by Spader, whose human identity inspired Ultron’s avatar) — holds Vision and the A.I. Jocasta (T’Nia Miller) captive to execute a plot for digital immortality. When Virgil fatally shoots Jocasta, a devastated Ultron murders Virgil and unleashes a lethal nanobot swarm on London. To stop the genocidal A.I., Vision traps them both within a creative WandaVision-style sitcom simulation dubbed UltraVision, forcing Ultron to confront the profound heartbreak of losing Jocasta — the A.I. companion he unwittingly fell for — which ultimately neutralizes the threat and causes both of their systems to collapse.

In the aftermath, Tommy and his twin brother Billy (Joe Locke) — who was last seen in Agatha — work together using their combined powers to successfully bring their father back to life. The finale also features a post-credits scene — not included in the screeners sent out to press — of Robert Downey Jr.’s Doctor Doom resurrecting Wanda, who had seemingly been crushed under a mountain amid her grief over losing Vision and their twins at the end of Multiverse of Madness. The Maximoff family reunion is on!

Calling from New York City just hours before the VisionQuest finale dropped on Disney+ on Tuesday, Matalas opened up below to THR about how the show became another meditation on grief in the MCU, why he decided to have Vision and Tommy reunite with Billy but not Wanda — and that ominous mid-credits scene with Ultron. As the former showrunner of Picard, Matalas also pays tribute to Patrick Stewart, who died Oct. 28 at the age of 86: “I’d like to remember him kind of where we left him [in Picard], which was at that poker table surrounded by his friends laughing.”

In addition to writing episodes one, two and eight, you also directed episodes seven and eight — which really crack Vision open emotionally and pay off his relationships with Tommy and Ultron. What was most important to you when you were figuring out how to land the plane, so to speak, on VisionQuest? Why was this the right ending in your mind?

I do think that all endings need to touch on the beginning in some way. So honoring WandaVision by going back to the sitcom format as sort of the last battle was always our north star from the beginning of the writers’ room. We had a few different versions of it, but it felt like the right way to end it rather than just doing a rock and sock ’em robot battle royale — which we do, so we give Marvel fans their popcorn. We thought it would be fun to play out the final struggle with these two within this father-son sitcom. [A reference to] Sanford and Son is one of the first images you see in the first episode [of UltraVision], so we knew we were heading into a kind of All in the Family, Sanford and Son dynamic between Ultron and Vision.

You mentioned that Jac did not want to be creatively involved in VisionQuest, but does she know that you paid homage to her with this show-within-a-show format?

No, as far as I know, she doesn’t have an idea.

There are so many fun little WandaVision Easter eggs in UltraVision, but I particularly loved flipping through all of the wacky episode titles. You came up with so many of them!

I actually did those in post. I think we had generated a list early on from a few different writers, but ultimately that came together in post. It’s the most fun ever. We kind of wish we saw every one of those episodes. I remember when we screened it for Kevin Feige, one of the questions I asked just to double check was, “Does UltraVision go on too long?” And he cut me off immediately and yelled, “No!” He’s like, “It could go on for another 90 minutes, and I would’ve watched every minute of it.” So it was a big swing. We were really scared. We didn’t know if that was going to work, and as of this moment, it hasn’t aired, so I don’t know if it has. (Laughs.) So we’ll see.

For all the theatrics of UltraVision, which turns out to be an ineffective way for Vision to appeal to Ultron’s better angels, Vision knows that the only way he can stop Ultron from using the nanobots as a weapon of mass destruction is by forcing him to feel the grief of losing Jocasta. What did you want those final one-on-one conversations between Vision and Ultron to represent?

I think Vision says it best, which is that we couldn’t process this alone, and that grief really is about opening up and bringing it to light, as is all pain and trauma. I hope that that’s the message people walk away with, which is you can’t really just bury it in your code. You really do have to face it head on, and it’s very hard to do it alone.

Why do you think Vision is the only one who is able to get through to Ultron in the end?

I think Vision is the only one he respects, whether that is because of Ultron’s own ego and that Vision was sort of his own vision, if you will, as to what he could be. But we always knew we wanted to take Ultron into a place from the comics. Ultron fell in love with Jocasta in the original comic books, and bringing him along into the same kind of journey that Vision had been facing all season felt like the right story for those two to truly understand each other by the end.

We had a few different versions [of Ultron’s final scene]. We had a deleted scene in which Jocasta actually was sitting with Ultron in the mansion at the end and had survived. And now, we just sort of hint that he’s going to, at some point, bring her back. And then the question is: Will that start the cycle all over again? Is he going to be doing the same thing Wanda did or Vision did, and not really face his grief and then find another way to bring back his loss? And would she even want that? So it felt like the right end of the circle, if you will.

You’re referring to the mid-credits scene of Ultron holding onto a hard drive labelled “Jocasta.” Why did you choose to include that final scene? Was that a directive from Marvel?

We were all so in love with Jocasta and [wanted] a promise that she would continue on in some way. Again, we had a deleted scene in which she magnificently survived. I think that scene will maybe one day see the light of day, but it sort of, in totality, robbed the finale of its punch a bit when we had it there. But there were no true directives from Marvel other than Tommy was going to meet Vision, and that by the end, cold white Vision would return to his original red self. That’s a pretty blank canvas to work from. Working with Marvel was truly wonderful and collaborative in every way.

Paul Bettany told me that Marvel’s initial plan was always to center VisionQuest around Vision and Tommy, but did you always plan to bring Billy back into the fold as well?

You had to. The end of Agatha was [Agatha and Billy saying], “Let’s go find Tommy.” I think it would’ve been terrible and not very satisfying to not see the boys reunited with their father by the end.

Did you ever consider introducing Billy earlier in the story, or were you always planning to bring him back to save Vision alongside Tommy in the finale?

We entertained it; we talked about it. But if Billy came back early, it robbed Tommy and Vision of their own story and alleviated too much tension too early, and wasn’t as emotional as when he comes back and saves the day in the last moment when they need him most. I didn’t want to do that to Billy. I didn’t want to make him a supporting character in someone else’s struggle, so really earning Billy felt like the right way, to us, to do it.

What were those days like on set for you to watch Paul, Ruaridh and Joe together on screen for the first time? Were both of Billy’s scenes filmed on the same day?

We had the scene with Tommy and Billy where they first connect psychically — that was on another day [before the father-sons reunion]. Those boys were so much fun to direct. We were in this tiny room that was about a thousand degrees because we lit about 800 candles. They were just so down to play. There are a couple of deleted fun bits that we came up with on the spot that will come out, but they had a great chemistry and we would be excited to see more of those two together in the future as well. But as far as the end where Billy returns to save the family there, I think maybe we had two hours to do all that. It’s television and you don’t have the luxury of the time, but it was great. Joe’s wonderful and so down to try new things, as is Ruaridh. We were fortunate that the father and sons had great chemistry.

In their final scene together, Tommy asks Vision if he thinks there is any chance, with the two of them and Billy still around, that they may see Wanda again. In a callback to WandaVision, Vision tells Tommy, “We have said goodbye before, so it stands to reason… we’ll say hello again.” Was that line your idea, or did it come out of a collaboration with Paul or the rest of the writers?

It was my idea. As I was writing it, even though that Vision wouldn’t know that Hex Vision said that, so much of his soul was the same that it felt right that he would say the same thing he said to Wanda at the end of WandaVision. And we had to ask the question! For me, you couldn’t not address, “Are we going to see Mom again?” I would be sad if I watched a show, with all this magic and reunion out there, where they weren’t asking that question of, could it be possible [to see her again] in this universe?

You have certainly left the door open for a Maximoff family reunion in the near future. Did you ever have any discussions with Paul or the rest of the creative team about Wanda returning in the VisionQuest finale?

Yes, of course. It’s a thing that comes up constantly. Paul and I did experiment with a moment as he was dying, and it just felt like an added element in a big emotional sweep that was really about Vision and Ultron, and Vision, Tommy and Billy. It’s such a big idea to have Wanda there that you no longer pay attention to the rest of the arcs that are playing out. But I do feel like she’s very much in the room. My brilliant editor, Drew Nichols, found this shot of Wanda from WandaVision where she looks and smiles, and when he thinks of her and he’s talking about how love always leads to loss, I felt like we had her. I felt like we had honored her, but it didn’t really work to have her back in a dreamy way at the end.

Ruaridh Mollica has affectionately referred to Tommy and Billy as the “queer twin brothers” of the MCU, and he has openly talked about the personal significance of a bisexual actor being cast to play a bisexual character in such an expansive fictional universe. Given what is already established in the comics, did you ever consider alluding to Tommy’s bisexuality more explicitly in the show? Was there any reason that you chose not to this time around?

We do have a lot of Easter eggs to it. We wanted to start with Lisa [Molinari, played by Lauren Morais] because in the comics he had this relationship with Lisa coming right out of juvie, which we thought was interesting. But there wasn’t really a lot of time for him to be exploring his sexuality with the stakes so high. We definitely put in some queer and bisexual-coded patches; [for instance] there are these patches on his green jacket in the third episode. Those are promises, I suppose, for future stories and relationships. But with eight episodes, you got to pick one, and the stakes were very high for him to be flirting. (Laughs.)

Billy comes back to save the day wearing his signature blue crown, but Tommy’s green Adidas jacket is the closest we ever get to seeing him wear a super suit this season.

We had discussions about a super suit, and sort of like the moment with Wanda, if it’s not organic, it feels jammed in. We just could not find a logical reason for this kid to have a super suit. (Laughs.) There was no way that was not cheesy to do it. So we tried to get the closest thing we can to normal real world wear to honor his look so that maybe one day down the line we’ll have a super suit.

The last time we see Vision and Tommy on screen together in the finale, they are talking about having dinner with Billy in Eastview. How do you think Vision feels now that he has reconnected with and effectively has to parent both of his boys as young men?

I mean, that’s the thing I want to see, right? The family, at least for the most part, minus one critical component, is reunited. So what is that like now? You get a little dose of it with him telling Tommy saying, “I know if your mom was here, she’d want you to continue your education.” So I think Vision’s got to go be a dad, and I would love nothing more than to see what that’s like.

Have you had any conversations yet about working on future installments of the MCU? Is there a world in which VisionQuest could be expanded into an ongoing series, or did you always see this as a limited series?

I will say that we have so, so many ideas. And if I were having those conversations, there’s no way I could say that I was having those conversations. But who would not want to see this family again?

I was so sad to hear about the passing of Patrick Stewart, with whom you worked closely on Star Trek: Picard, and I’m very sorry for your loss. A lot of people on social media have thanked you for giving them the final gift of revisiting and saying goodbye to Patrick’s Picard, even though no one knew for sure that that would be the last time he’d play the character. Given that you began your career working on Star Trek: Enterprise, what did working on Picard with him mean to you personally, and how would you like to remember him?

I’d like to remember him kind of where we left him, which was at that poker table surrounded by his friends laughing. I was lucky enough to write and direct the last few moments of Captain Picard. It’s an honor I didn’t feel like I deserved, but feel blessed to have. The last scene with all of them, I really wanted to capture who he was around that cast. They were all dear friends and family in every way to him. What I did was I just let them actually play poker and joke and have fun. All of those smiles, all of those laughs from everyone and especially Patrick, were genuine. I wanted the fans in the world to see that because it’s an extraordinary thing to be around a cast like that, that truly loves each other that way.

I wanted to leave Captain Picard for everyone with all of them in a moment of joy and reunion, as opposed to him dying on the bridge of a starship or something like that. I like a happy ending — not always, but specifically in this case, this is how I wanted to leave that cast. It’s very kind for people to thank me, but I just played a small part in this universe and was honored to do it.

Do you remember the first time you met him? Was it when you were working as a PA on the Paramount lot and driving him around on golf carts?

Yeah, that’s exactly what it was. You do your research! (Laughs.) My first job in Hollywood was as a production assistant on Star Trek: Voyager, and I believe they started to shoot Star Trek: Insurrection within my first month. Merri Howard, who was my boss and mentor, pulled me from the television show to work on that movie for a day and just take care of Patrick and drive him around and get him coffee and orange juice. And going from that kid who would sneak on to the bridge of the Enterprise E, to bringing him back to the Enterprise D, is such a surreal, unbelievable journey. It’s a very Hollywood dream come true, and I just feel lucky to have been part of Star Trek for so long and hope to continue someday with more of it.

All episodes of VisionQuest are now streaming on Disney+.

#713. Adam Conover May Be Getting Vulnerable on Stage, But He’s Still Riled Up About a Hollywood in Decline

The comedian and writer's latest stand-up special, 'Big Divorce Energy,' talks about an unexpected dip into personal material and the merger impact he says we're only starting: "We tried to avert the asteroid coming and we failed."

There are two Adam Conovers. One, the guy you probably know the best, played a satirical know-it-all on Adam Ruins Everything and has gone on to become a champion of the Hollywood working class. Other Adam, the guy he says a lot of people don’t know as well, is a touring stand-up whose recent demise of a 15-year-relationship has inspired him to delve to some real personal material.

The latter lays everything pretty bare in Big Divorce Energy, his recent hour that dropped Oct. 23 on his YouTube channel. It’s a pivot for anyone who just knows him from his TV work or his penchant for opining on podcasts. “I had always directed my comedy outwards,” says Conover, “talking about the world and things in the world, issues, history, politics, science, informing people of things. I had never really turned inward.” Related Stories TV Lana Condor, Anthony De La Torre Team for Rom-Com Microseries for Fetch (Exclusive) Business Piers Morgan Wants to Conquer America's Midterm Election Coverage

Looking inward involved candor about dating and sex in the wake of his split from illustrator Lisa Hanawalt, who worked on BoJack Horseman and created the Netflix series Tuca & Bertie. They remain friends and Hanawalt even gave her ex a particularly good note as he was refining the set, helping him move some things around to find the right joke to land on: a delightfully crude punchline that may offend the always even-keeled DC fandom.

“I’m on this quest to understand myself and my sexuality, especially what drives straight men, men who grew up straight or identify as straight in America,” he says. “Because I think that our sexuality is kind of the great unexamined frontier… I think straight men are the most sexually repressed people.”

In any conversation with Conover — and you can listen to the full thing on Spotify, Amazon Music or Apple — one can’t help but dig into his thoughts on the industry. During the 2023 strikes, he became one of the most biggest advocates for Hollywood unions and outspoken members of the WGA. He has railed against merger culture and, even a month after it was formalized, a post calling Skydance’s once looming acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery a “disaster” is still pinned atop his Instagram page. Now that it’s all done and dusted, he has not changed his tune. “We tried to avert the asteroid coming and we failed,” he says. “Now it’s coming and we’re all gonna face the consequences.”

His frequently strong words for the people who essentially write his checks beg the question: has he seen a negative impact on his work? Conover doesn’t see it that way, and he’s the first to say that everyone but those at the very top agree with him. “There’s a long tradition of my type of comedian being antagonistic towards the network brass,” he says. “On Adam Ruins Everything, we talked about the cable monopolies and advertising and stuff like that. That’s why the audience likes me. And so if they want to work with me, to get my audience, then that’s what they’re gonna get.”

But Conover also knows that those companies aren’t buying his particular brand of comedy at the moment, which is why he elected to self-release the new hour instead of shopping it around.

“The companies have given up on what I do and sort of pushed me to new media,” says Conover. “David Zaslav could [have given] a living wage and health insurance for people to write a bunch of comedy that he gets to own and monetize, but he and David Ellison and Ted Sarandos don’t want to do that anymore. Instead, I’ve got to build my own business on YouTube.”

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 10, 2013, Europe's GOCE satellite fell to Earth after four years in orbit mapping the planet's gravitational field.

GOCE, its name was short for Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer, launched in 2009 on a mission to map Earth's gravity like never before. But despite that successful mission, it was doomed in 2013 when it ran out of fuel.

At the time, controllers weren't sure where GOCE would fall back to Earth. Some people worried that it might crash into a populated area. However, the small spacecraft broke up in the atmosphere and didn't cause any property damage.

It disintegrated about 50 miles above the Falkland Islands in the South Atlantic Ocean. The European Space Agency called the mission a success. GOCE lasted far longer than expected. It showed small variations in Earth's gravity, mapped the structure of Earth's crust and mantle, and tracked ocean currents.

The GOCE satellite was a sleek spacecraft, with fins covered in solar panels that gave it a futuristic design. In fact, its look earned it a pretty cool nickname.

"GOCE's sleek, elegant aerodynamic design — responsible for it being dubbed the 'Ferrari of space' — immediately set it apart from most other satellites,." ESA officials said in a description.

There was more than looks behind GOCE's design. In order to generate the best map ever of Earth's gravitational field, GOCE had to fly in an orbit so low — just 139 miles (224 kilometers) — it needed to counteract the drag from the gossamer thin atmosphere of Earth at that altitude. The International Space Station orbits Earth at nearly twice that altitude.

GOCE was powered by an xenon ion engine that allowed to maintain its low orbit for four years. Once it ran out of fuel, the 1-ton satellite could not maintain its position in space, leading to a fiery plunge to Earth.

The large size of GOCE — it weighed 2,425 pounds (1,100 kilograms) and was 17 feet (5.3 meters) long and 3.2 feet (1 m) wide — made its reentry stand out, particularly since at least 25% of the satellite was expected to reach the Earth's surface.

After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#711. A mysterious 93-billion-mile cosmic structure may be the wreckage of colliding worlds

A mysterious structure stretching roughly 93 billion miles across space is giving astronomers new clues about the violent events that shape young planetary systems. Known as the "Cat's Tail," this enormous cloud of dark material lies about 63 light-years from Earth, in the faint constellation Pictor (which is Latin for "painter"). For the past two years, its unusual appearance and uncertain origins have puzzled scientists.

The structure is part of a vast disk of dust and debris surrounding Beta Pictoris, a young star system that resembles our own solar system during its early development. Now, using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have captured previously hidden details of the Cat's Tail in visible light for the first time.

The discovery is described in a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Led by University of Arizona planetary scientist Arin Avsar, the research team combined the new Hubble images with observations spanning more than 14 years. Their findings provide a clearer picture of the structure's composition, location, and shape, along with additional evidence that a massive collision may have created it.

A Possible Collision Between Pluto-Sized Worlds

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies - think something like Pluto," said Avsar, a doctoral student working with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory.

"Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

The mystery becomes even more interesting when viewed in the context of how planetary systems form.

Today, our solar system appears relatively orderly. Planets follow established paths around the Sun, while many smaller rocky objects occupy "designated" regions such as the asteroid belt. But 4.6 billion years ago, the situation was dramatically different.

A young sun was surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust. Rocky objects repeatedly collided, sometimes breaking apart and sometimes combining into larger bodies. Over time, some accumulated enough material to become planets, while countless others were destroyed or scattered.

Astronomers study younger systems like Beta Pictoris because they offer an opportunity to observe processes that unfolded in our own cosmic neighborhood billions of years ago. Its debris disk, consisting of dust and fragments left behind during planetary development, is believed to be approaching the final stages of planet formation.

Why Hubble Could Finally See the Mysterious Cat's Tail

One of the most intriguing questions about the Cat's Tail is why it was previously detectable in infrared light but so difficult to observe in visible light.

The answer may lie in the unusual material that makes up the enormous structure.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

Organic refractory material consists of complex carbon compounds that can withstand relatively harsh conditions in space. Because these compounds absorb much of the visible light that strikes them, they can make the surrounding dust appear exceptionally dark.

The Hubble observations also support another unusual finding: the Cat's Tail appears to be composed of extremely small, surprisingly porous dust particles.

Individual grains measure only about a micron across, roughly one millionth of a meter. Yet instead of being compact and solid, they appear remarkably "fluffy," with substantial empty space within their structures.

The scale of the entire cloud is difficult to imagine. It may stretch as far as 1,000 astronomical units, with one astronomical unit (AU) defined as the average distance between Earth and the Sun. That corresponds to approximately 93 billion miles, or the equivalent of lining up around 200 trillion house cats from tail to nose.

"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

How a Violent Collision Could Create Fluffy Cosmic Dust

If the Cat's Tail really formed when large planetary bodies smashed into each other, researchers still need to explain how that destruction produced such tiny, porous particles.

One possibility is that the collision was powerful enough to vaporize some of the material involved.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," said co-author Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory.

In this scenario, the intense impact would have transformed solid carbon material into gas. As the material cooled, it could have condensed back into solid particles with unusually open, lightweight structures.

However, the precise process remains uncertain, and additional observations will be needed to determine whether this explanation is correct.

A 93-Billion-Mile Structure With an Unexpected Shape

The new research also challenges previous assumptions about where the Cat's Tail extends in space.

By combining visible light observations from Hubble with infrared measurements from the James Webb Space Telescope, the researchers used computer modeling to reconstruct the structure's possible three-dimensional arrangement.

Earlier observations suggested that the Cat's Tail extended outward from Beta Pictoris and far behind the star from Earth's perspective. Because the surrounding debris disk is viewed nearly edge-on, it was difficult to determine how much of the structure extended away from us rather than across our field of view.

The new analysis points to a different explanation.

"We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat's Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it," Avsar said. "It's essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it."

This suggests the structure may be spread mainly across the sky as seen from Earth, rather than projecting deep into space behind the star.

The revised geometry gives astronomers a better understanding of where the dust is located and could help them reconstruct the event that produced it.

Hubble Discovers a Strange Warp Caused by a Giant Planet

The Cat's Tail was not the only unusual feature revealed by the new observations.

Using Hubble in a different observational configuration, Avsar and his colleagues also identified an unexpected distortion in the broad halo of dust surrounding Beta Pictoris.

The researchers suspect this strange warp may be caused by the gravitational influence of Beta Pic b, one of three planets in the system.

Beta Pic b is a massive gas giant estimated to be about 10 times the mass of Jupiter. Its powerful gravity may be disturbing the surrounding debris, altering the paths of dust particles, comets, and other icy objects across enormous distances.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units."

The finding highlights how giant planets can shape their environments far beyond their immediate orbits.

A Glimpse Into Our Solar System's Violent Past

For researchers, Beta Pictoris offers more than an opportunity to investigate an unusual cosmic structure. It may also provide a window into the early history of our own solar system.

Consider the Kuiper Belt, the distant region beyond Neptune that contains Pluto and numerous other icy bodies.

When the Kuiper Belt was only about 20 million years old, astronomers believe it was much more crowded than it is today. It may have contained hundreds of objects comparable in size to Pluto.

Over billions of years, the gravitational influence of the solar system's outer giant planets likely changed that environment dramatically. By disturbing the orbits of smaller bodies, these planets may have pushed many objects into new regions or expelled them from the solar system entirely, effectively "clearing out" much of the original population.

The strange dust tail and newly identified warp around Beta Pictoris may offer clues to similar processes unfolding in another planetary system.

By studying these distant structures, astronomers hope to better understand how violent collisions, migrating debris, and the immense gravity of giant planets helped transform the chaos of the early solar system into the planetary arrangement we see today.
