#710. ‘The Odyssey’ Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs

Matt Damon moderated a crew Q&A after the premiere of Christopher Nolan’s 75-minute making-of documentary.

That was my first thought after watching “Behind the Scenes of ‘The Odyssey,’” a 75-minute documentary chronicling the making of Christopher Nolan’s $1.8 billion blockbuster, which premiered Tuesday night at the Spielberg Theater on the Universal Studios lot.

“I have absolutely mastered the art of talking a lot and revealing absolutely nothing,” Nolan joked as he introduced the film. “And so I’m told I need to get out of the way.” Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings

Most viewers won’t see the full version screened Tuesday. The 75-minute cut was a one-time presentation, while a shorter version will be included with the film’s digital home release, arriving Nov. 17. Universal has not announced which portions will make the cut.

After the screening, star Matt Damon, who plays Odysseus, moderated an hourlong conversation with 12 department heads: producer Emma Thomas, production designer Ruth De Jong, editor Jennifer Lame, composer and songwriter Ludwig Göransson, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson, special effects supervisor Scott Fisher, costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, casting director John Papsidera, supervising sound editor Craig Henighan, production sound mixer Willie Burton, head of makeup Luisa Abel and head of hair Gloria Casny.

The room was packed with guild voters and social media influencers, including comedian and actor Evan M. Williams. Afterward, the crowd spilled into the lobby, where exhibits on the film’s artisan achievements awaited and multiple conversations and selfies began.

The premiere kicks off two weeks of Universal awards-season screenings for “The Odyssey,” the highest-grossing film of Nolan’s career. The studio is campaigning the film across all categories, aiming to match or break the record 16 Oscar nominations Ryan Coogler’s “Sinners” earned earlier this year.

The campaign continues Wednesday, when Robert Downey Jr. moderates an Imax 70mm screening at the TCL Chinese Theatre, followed Thursday by Guillermo del Toro at AMC Universal CityWalk. On Nov. 17, Steven Spielberg sits down with Nolan at the DGA Theater, the same day “The Odyssey” arrives on digital.

Nolan is also paying it forward Saturday, moderating a Q&A with “Digger” director Alejandro G. Iñárritu.

Here are eight of the most revealing moments from the documentary and the Q&A.

Matt Damon didn’t loop a single line on “The Odyssey”

Damon revealed that he did not have to re-record a single line of dialogue for “The Odyssey,” a rarity for a production of this scale. “I did not loop a line for this movie,” he said onstage, turning to legendary production sound mixer Burton to ask how he pulled it off.

Burton explained Nolan’s strict rules. “There’s no ADR with Chris,” he said. “Does not want to do ADR, and he also wants the boom mic to be on a cable.”

The commitment to capturing sound on set extended to the ship itself. Burton recalled being sent below deck during the production, where he ran cables under the floorboards and mounted microphones on the hull. During storm sequences, water poured down on him. He also became the ship’s unofficial snack clerk.

“I’m trying to do sound now, and one of the guys is, ‘Can you hand me potato chips?’” Burton recalled getting boisterous laughter from the crowd.

The documentary also shows how much attention went into the film’s sound design. Henighan sent a crew to record the ship for real, including every oar stroke. Re-recording mixers Gary Rizzo and Kevin O’Connell note that nearly everything in the mix is organic, from gongs forged by human hands to the army’s actual screams.

Nolan wanted nothing to do with the “very cartoony, very unthreatening” Cyclops sequences of decades past. His visual inspiration was Francisco Goya’s “Saturn Devouring His Son,” particularly its blank, indifferent face.

De Jong suggested turning the creature’s single eye sideways and centering it. Jackson then conducted a simple test: He filmed actor Bill Irwin, who plays Polyphemus, improvising in a dark Universal office with a desk lamp on the floor. Jackson digitally moved one of Irwin’s eyes to the center of his face and painted out the other.

“It was quite phenomenal, actually, how effective it was,” Jackson said.

The documentary also reveals that the giant creature was initially represented by a crude stick-figure puppet. The original plan was to shoot the sequence on an L.A. soundstage late in production. But after Nolan and De Jong scouted Greece and found a real cave, the team had to finish the puppet and get it standing on a Greek mountain within two months.

The production ultimately built only the creature’s rigid parts around the simpler structure. “Because of the way that we were forced to make it in a much simpler way, it actually worked much better,” he said.

Tom Holland asked for a shorter skirt to look taller, and Robert Pattinson wanted a long wig. Both were rejected by Nolan.

Thomas, Nolan’s producing partner and wife, described two versions of the director: one who demands the impossible during preparation and another who becomes “incredibly pragmatic” once shooting starts.

The documentary offers a running list of things Nolan won’t allow.

Marking her first Nolan film, Casny received a request from Robert Pattinson, who plays Antinous, for a long wig. The actor called her on the first day of fittings while she was standing next to Nolan and Thomas. “I didn’t even know how he got my number,” Casny recalled. “The answer was no.”

Holland tells a story in the documentary about his first costume fitting, where he quietly asked Mirojnick to shorten his skirt a bit so he’d look taller. Six weeks later, the alteration was done and the costume went before Nolan. “Two seconds into taking in the costume, he was like, ‘How come the skirt is shorter?’” Holland says.

Nolan’s attention to detail is paramount which Damon even chimed in to highlight. He recalled a day on “Oppenheimer” when a missing hat delayed the company on a moving train for half an hour. Thomas jumped in with the obvious lesson learned: “He does not like hats.”

And when Henighan presented a particularly graphic, squelchy sound design for the Samantha Morton’s Circe sequence, Nolan wasn’t interested. He preferred dry bones cracking and knuckles popping.

Nolan told his Marine Coordinator, ‘I Don’t Accept That’ about physics.

Damon recalled a moment in Scotland when the sea tore apart one of the production’s boats during the Laestrygonian sequence. Marine coordinator Neil Andrea explained that the transom and hull had been ripped out and that getting the vessel ready for the next day was “literally impossible.”

“And Chris turned to Neil and said, ‘I don’t accept that,’” Damon recalled. “And somehow that thing was floating the next day, and we shot on it.”

Thomas, gamely defending her husband, added: “I promise you, he’s more pragmatic than that.”

The sea was the production’s most stubborn adversary. Nolan admitted that he had privately hoped to minimize boat time while writing the script. “But it’s ‘The Odyssey,’” he said. “Of course, we’re going to be on this boat for months.”

Andrea’s team converted Viking ship replicas from Scandinavia into Greek warships, hiding small engines inside them. The storm destruction sequences were eventually filmed on the Universal backlot, with jet engines blasting the ship on a gimbal.

The production’s logistical challenges extended to the Trojan horse itself. In Morocco, Nolan moved the start date up two days while the enormous prop was still sitting in crates at customs.

“I’m like, ‘What? The horse is in boxes in customs.’ And he’s like, ‘Yeah, anyways, carry on,’” De Jong recalled.

When the crew finally planted the horse in the sand for the opening shot, the incoming tide knocked it over. Nolan’s response? “Great. Well, I’m gonna shoot this tomorrow.”

The fall of Troy was built practically, with a 2.5-acre city constructed between late December and early February. Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema wanted to light the entire film with fire, so he designed hundreds of LED fixtures, nicknamed “pyrahedrons,” calibrated to the color of firelight.

Nolan sees his entire filmography inside Homer

The documentary’s opening stretch plays like a Nolan master class, with Damon recalling the conversation that started the project. Nolan caught up with him for 10 or 15 minutes and said two words: “The Odyssey.”

Nolan describes Homer’s poem as containing all of Western literature, including the DNA of his own films. Adapting it meant recognizing “that’s where I got that thing from ‘Interstellar,’ or that’s where ‘The Dark Knight’ comes from.”

Rather than imitate the Romantic-era paintings and Hollywood epics of the 1950s and ’60s that defined the genre, Nolan applied the grounded approach of “The Dark Knight,” “Inception” and “Interstellar” to Greek mythology.

Ludwig Göransson built the score around 35 bronze gongs

Damon said that whenever he asked what Göransson was working on, Nolan answered with one word: gongs.

The composer explained that he shut himself in his studio during the Los Angeles fires, surrounded by about 35 bronze gongs and spent 10 days learning to write for them. He had heard gongs before, he noted, “in the theme song for ‘Mortal Kombat.’”

From there, Göransson sought out musicians who played the ancient aulos and lyre. He also traveled to southern Albania to record iso-polyphonic folk singing.

The documentary’s music chapter ends at Abbey Road with vocalist James Blake. The end-credits song, “When I’m Home,” came about because Göransson wanted the film to finish the song started by the bard, played by Travis Scott. The track uses Scott’s original vocal recording from the movie.

Nearly 7,000 extras were put through hair and makeup and Matt Damon performs pullups.

The documentary makes clear that grounding Greek mythology in reality required enormous detail. More than 80 hair and makeup artists worked in Morocco, and just under 7,000 background performers passed through fittings.

The teams erased every modern tell, from tattoos and earring holes to the shape of women’s eyebrows.

Mirojnick also created distinct visual identities for the principal characters.

Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, wears bright colors because, as the actress explains, she isn’t a widow and keeps dressing as if her husband will return. Telemachus (Tom Holland) transitions from boy to man through increasingly bright, light armor, while Antinous wears a leopard pelt.

As for casting, Papsidera says Nolan once described Homer as writing “the Marvel films of his time,” so the actors had to be the superstars of ours. Odysseus’ warriors, though, needed real bodies. “You don’t want it to look like, you know, 2025 bodybuilding,” Papsidera says. “They weren’t taking peptides.”

Papsidera, whose work ends before cameras roll, had his doubts. “This pragmatic Chris, I’d like to meet sometime,” he cracked, adding that he doesn’t even get a copy of the script to keep. He also joked with Damon of the pecking order: “No movie without us, buddy.”

And most notably, points to the short prep time that left him roughly 62 days to cast about 60 actors.

Damon, meanwhile, was well aware of the physical demands of playing Odysseus. Filmed doing pullups on a ladder, the actor offers a candid assessment of the production. “I’m 54 years old, and I knew this was going to be really physical.”

Near the end of the doc, Damon delivers the line that may become the campaign’s rallying cry. “My whole life was kind of leading up to this movie, and I don’t know how long we’re going to get to make movies this way.”

Onstage, Thomas turned the spotlight on the moderator, making sure voters know the movie couldn’t exist without its star, who has yet to win an acting Oscar. “I cannot believe we did it,” she said, crediting Damon for being “on set, on time with the best attitude every morning.”

Damon passed the praise back down the row. “I’ve never seen more asked of a crew, never,” Damon concluded. “And I don’t think I ever could again.” Then he pauses chuckling. “That didn’t come out right.”

#709. Iconic first image of black hole holds up to scrutiny

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Physicists used an algorithm to combine telescope measurements of a black hole in a different way to the original analysis.Credit: S. Lai, N. Thyagarajan, O. I. Wong, and F. Diakogiannis; Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration wowed the world in 2019 with the first picture ever taken of a black hole’s shadow. Some researchers were unconvinced, arguing that the circular shape seen in that shot was an artefact of the team’s image-reconstruction techniques. Now, an independent group has reanalysed the EHT data, and its results, published on 11 November in Nature — including new images of the black hole — largely corroborate the original findings1.

To image black holes, the international EHT collaboration stitches together data it collects simultaneously from an array of ground-based radio telescopes that stretches across several continents. The reconstruction is extremely challenging, but in principle the result is an image with the same level of detail, or resolution, that would be achieved with a single radio dish as wide as Earth.

Although blurry, the EHT shot of a supermassive black hole at the centre of the M87 galaxy was consistent with astrophysical models based on Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which first predicted the existence of black holes. The image had a bright ring of roughly the correct radius, given what was known about the size of the black hole, with a darker disk at the centre.

However, starting in 20222, Junichiro Makino, an astrophysicist at Kobe University in Japan, and his collaborators began questioning those conclusions. By applying one of the data-analysis techniques the EHT collaboration had used, but with slightly different assumptions, Makino’s team obtained a different result. Their image shows a glob of radio emissions rather than a ring.

#708. Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.

As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.

Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.

Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.

Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.

However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.

The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.

A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow

The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."

"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.

Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.

Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.

For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.

The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.

Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.

The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.

The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.

"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"

This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.

In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.

Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.

"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.

A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean

Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.

Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.

Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.

The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.

Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."

The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

#707. A Rom-Com Connoisseur Goes Into Business With the True Story of a Sex Toy Saleswoman

Andy Tennant and Jessica Alba take on the task of empowering the sex-curious women of the Bible Belt in the AFM-bound 'The Fun Lady.'

Andy Tennant has always been led by the strong women in his life.

The American filmmaker and screenwriter is certainly an expert in the rom-com department, having helmed 2002’s Sweet Home Alabama with Reese Witherspoon and the Will Smith-led Hitch in 2005, two undeniable titans of the genre.

But for Tennant, who also directed 2008’s Fool’s Gold and 2010’s The Bounty Hunter, his latest project has never encompassed that connection to female resilience so well. “I’ve always felt in literature and everything else that female characters are so much more interesting than male characters, especially in movies,” he begins to The Hollywood Reporter. “Because male characters and [male] movie stars, their character doesn’t learn anything. Women’s stories… They’re so much more. They’re allowed to be eager, to be more vulnerable, to be more curious. And those stories I’m naturally drawn to.” Related Stories Movies China's Film Industry Arrives at AFM on a Domestic High Movies Can Constantin Survive Its Own Parent Company?

It’s befitting, then, that The Fun Lady — produced by Highland Film Group and headed to AFM — is not only getting the Andy Tennant treatment, but honoring one of the wildest true stories in the sex-toy industry. Linda Brewer, then 59, was the subject of a New York Times Magazine story in 2004 titled “Everything a Happily Married Bible Belt Woman Always Wanted to Know About Sex but Was Afraid to Ask.” It chronicles her rise from Arkansas high school dropout to becoming one of the top sellers for Passion Parties, a California-based company whose products included edible lotions, sex manuals, erotic games, lingerie and, crucially, an array of vibrators. Sure, she made sales of up to $140,000 in a single year, but Brewer also did the unthinkable: Smashed taboos and empowered the sex-curious, unsatisfied women of the Bible Belt.

In The Fun Lady, Brewer is depicted by superstar Jessica Alba (also producing the feature under her Metalmark Entertainment banner). She plays golden girl Mora, who retreats to her parents’ small Arkansas hometown when her picture-perfect life falls apart. Here, jobs are scarce, and gossip is a way of life. Desperate for a fresh start, she begins selling sex toys. The only problem is her absolute ignorance about pleasure, having never experienced an orgasm. Against all odds, Mora becomes “The Fun Lady,” crashing living rooms, shocking church ladies, and turning awkward sales parties into the hottest invitation in town. Along the way, she ignites a sexual revolution among women who have spent their lives pretending everything is fine.

Tennant, upon reading Mark Steilen’s (Tag, Shameless) script, was instantly hooked. “I thought, ‘You got to be kidding me!'” he recalls, chuckling to THR. “It’s such a lovely movie.” It’s not a romantic comedy, but he believed it to be very Sweet Home Alabama-adjacent. “The fact that it was based on a true story… I just found it incredible, and what a great jumping-off point for a story about not only human sexuality but relationships and the suppression of female sexual identity.” Importantly, for Tennant, it isn’t “comedy with a capital C.” The Fun Lady grapples with the human condition and the relationships that inform it, which, for him, “is what I’ve tried to do in pretty much every movie I’ve done.”

With production set to kick off early next year, Tennant is relieved to have a professional like Alba on board. “Casting has basically made my job a whole lot easier,” he says, reflecting on the myriad of A-listers that have stood in front of his camera. “[The Fun Lady] doesn’t need to cost any more than it’s going to cost. But we needed somebody who really got the material and understood that it wasn’t going to be a comedy with a bunch of cheap laughs. And Jessica, in my first conversation with her, [I could tell] she’s incredibly smart.”

Alba is not unlike the real-life person her role is inspired by: tenacious and a natural businesswoman. “She’s an entrepreneur,” Tennant continues. “She’s made an enormous success out of her business [consumer goods brand The Honest Company], and her conversations with me were [I was] like, ‘Oh, wow, I really need to be on my toes here.’ Because she takes it incredibly seriously. It is a comedy but there’s an awful lot of thematic issues that she really wants to bring to the fore,” he says, for example, women’s sexuality and marriages that play out “in a selfish way.”

Tennant is more than happy to let Alba — and a slew of cast members THR is not yet privy to the identities of — take the lead. “This is not false humility, but most of the time I try and stay out of the way,” he explains. “I set the camera and create an environment where everybody feels safe and willing to try things, and lot of what I love about prep actually is the conversations that happen with all the individual characters about what they’re thinking, what they’re afraid of, what they’re not sure of, and it challenges me.” Rather poetically, he actually likens the experience to heading up an orchestra: “We’ve got the bassoon and we’ve got the double bass and we’ve got the French horn and the violin. What we’re trying to create is a group that when they’re all together, has a wonderful harmony.”

What would have been a real weapon at their disposal during the shoot is the input of Brewer, who Tennant confirms has passed away. Although, he says, she was involved “quite a lot” with Steilen during the writing process. “Mark pursued the story. He spoke to her many, many times. And I know that her children are still very much wanting to see this movie made,” says the filmmaker.

And with Alba, he’s attempted to honor Brewer’s legacy by fleshing out the women of this story as much as possible. “We’ve tried to expand on the many women and the passion parties — no two are alike,” Tennant maintains. “The relationships are different. Their issues are different, and so we wanted to explore a lot of that. Somebody might not relate to Jessica’s character as much as they might relate to somebody else, and go, ‘Oh, I was there once in that relationship,’ or ‘I’m still in it.’ It doesn’t matter if it’s 1988 or 2000 or 2027. Sometimes, it’s hard to say what you want, say what you need, and it definitely affects your relationship.”

And if he’s honest with himself? Tennant didn’t have very many edits at all. “I actually said to Mark, ‘This is one of the few scripts that I’ve ever been offered that I haven’t had to do a ton of triage or work or rewrite or bring in other writers.’ In this case,” he adds, “the material was really, really strong.”

And when Tennant, the man behind the onscreen love affairs of Matthew Perry and Salma Hayek (in Fools Rush In) or Drew Barrymore and Dougray Scott (Ever After), casts his mind back to some of his favorite comedies of all time, such as Tootsie or the work of Sydney Pollack and Mike Nichols, what gives them their standout status is that unsuspecting warmth — and vital messaging — underneath those layers of fun and frill. “If I can just aspire to that level of intimacy and honesty and humor and real, honest character work…” says Tennant, trailing off. “If you laugh, you laugh. But maybe you’ll leave the theater thinking a little bit more about your relationship.”

#706. Scarlett Johansson Has Gotten Such Bad Studio Movie Offers That She’s Told Execs: ‘I Don’t Think You Should Make This… It Seems Irresponsible’

Scarlett Johansson told the Los Angeles Times on her “Piper Tiger” press tour that she sometimes gets acting offers from major Hollywood studios that leave her questioning why the movie is even being made. The Oscar nominee’s studio output in recent years has been dominated by her role as Black Widow in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Her last Hollywood tentpole was 2025’s “Jurassic World Rebirth.”

“Am I making something that other people want to see? Is there an audience for this movie? I’m not making a movie just for me,” Johansson said about the thought process behind selecting roles. “Sometimes I get studio projects that I have to say, ‘I don’t think you should make this. I don’t know who you’re making this for. It seems irresponsible to make this.’” Related Stories Jon Stewart Breaks Down Trump’s ‘60 Minutes’ Interview: 'Young Man, Was That Sass?' A Day in the Life at 'The Daily Show': Jon Stewart Hypes Up Writers' Room in Behind-the-Scenes Video (EXCLUSIVE)

While her latest release, “Paper Tiger,” is an independent drama (it was picked up by Neon shortly before its world premiere at the Cannes Film Festival earlier this year), Johansson spent much of this year shooting back-to-back studio tentpoles “The Exorcist: Martyrs” (in theaters March 12, 2027) and “The Batman 2” (Feb. 18, 2028). Next up in her production schedule is “Scapegoat,” the new movie from “Midsommar” and “Eddington” filmmaker Ari Aster. The project is backed by A24 and co-stars Jude Law.

“I don’t know what it is either,” Johansson told the Times about the movie. “I’ll have more information for you after a few weeks. The script is just so intense. It has this immediacy to it that is really different. I’ve never read anything like it before. [My husband] was like, ‘What are you reading?’ Because I kept going, ‘Oh, my God!’”

Johansson did not name which studio offers were total busts, but she has been open in previous interviews about the studio movies she desperately wanted. One such movie was Alfonso Cuarón’s “Gravity” (the role went to Sandra Bullock) and another was “Iron Man 2” (Emily Blunt originally landed the role of Black Widow but had to drop out due to scheduling conflicts). In a previous Variety interview, Johansson cited losing out on both movies as the moment she went into crisis mode as an actor.

“I got turned down for two roles — the first was ‘Iron Man 2’ and then the other one was ‘Gravity,’” Johansson said. “I had wanted that role so much. It was sort of the straw that broke the camel’s back. I felt really frustrated and hopeless. Like, ‘Am I doing the right job?’ The work I was being offered felt deeply unfulfilling. I think I was offered every Marilyn Monroe script ever. I was like, ‘Is this the end of the road creatively?’”

Johansson has long traded off major Hollywood studio movies with edgier indie fare. She’s moving into shooting Aster’s “Scapegoat” after wrapping production on the Warner Bros.-backed “The Batman 2,” her role in which remains a mystery.

“It was very hard to figure out,” Johansson told “Entertainment Tonight” earlier this month about the superhero sequel. “I don’t know why, whether it was just the role or it was just where I am in my life, but it was just hard to crack it. And that’s all I can say about it.”

#705. Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

In a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology, suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza.

The discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk.

A Surprising Connection Between Flu Vaccines and Alzheimer's

Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050.

Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study, a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older.

Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences.

Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published new research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk?

The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them.

"The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused."

Why Older Adults Receive Stronger Flu Shots

As people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors.

To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus.

The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines.

Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available.

"I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said.

Annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment.

Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation.

Previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits.

Another practical issue made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead.

This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations.

"So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said.

Nearly 200,000 Adults Reveal a Significant Difference

To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older.

The results showed that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation.

The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%.

The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine.

These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise important questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease.

However, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection.

What the Findings Could Mean for Alzheimer's Prevention

With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk.

The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely new treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults.

The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an important consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease.

For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention.

Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is currently a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study.

Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin.

Researchers from the McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics at UTHealth Houston also participated. They included Xiaoqian Jiang, PhD, associate vice president for medical AI, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and Christopher Sarofim Family Professor in Biomedical Informatics and Bioengineering; Yejin Kim, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence; Luyao Chen, researcher; and Yaobin Ling, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow.

Materials provided by University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

In any respectable audiobook project, finding the names of Andy Weir ("The Martian," "Project Hail Mary") and Benjamin Percy ("The Ninth Metal," "Wolverine") attached would elicit intense fan interest, but add the superstar vocal talents of Anthony Mackie ("Avengers: Infinity War," "Avengers: Doomsday"), Ariana DeBose ("West Side Story"), and John Leguizamo ("Ice Age"), and it catapults this sonic odyssey into the stratosphere.

Such is the case with "Exoplanet," Audible Original’s new 7-episode science fiction audio drama executive produced by Weir and penned by Percy. Its planet-hopping space disaster narrative sees the crew of the starship Wild Blue Yonder hit a quantum anomaly, forcing their ship to crash-land onto a deadly exoplanet. All is not as it seems, though, as each crew member arrives in a different era on the same world.

We hooked up with Mackie, DeBose, and Lequizamo to learn more about this renaissance of audio dramas and what attracted them to board Weir's sci-fi thriller.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Mackie voices Chief Engineer Jeff Shaw. His attraction to the imaginative genre began at an early age thanks to some cool family friends while growing up in the Big Easy.

"My brother went to college at Morehouse," he tells SPACE. "I was like 8, and he was 18. He’d always bring friends home, because New Orleans is a party city, so they'd come over and get drunk. But one of his friends gave me a book by Walter Mosley and one by Octavia Butler, and I got hooked into sci-fi and the future."

"From 'Back to the Future' to 'Aliens,' the future was such an idea of what was going to be out there. Now we’re living it," reveals Mackie. "It’s very important to me as a human being to have that construct as a part of my career. The only thing more arrogant than wanting to be president is standing up and saying, 'Yeah, I can go to space.' That sounds crazy to me."

Leguizamo's New York City childhood was influenced by absorbing classic radio dramas of the past, which primed him for this special Audible project.

“It was Anthony and Ariana being in it that really pumped me up, and of course Andy Weir," he recalls regarding his portrayal of Science Officer Logan Bowers. "Then when I got the theme, that it was something relevant today and makes you think about computers and technology taking over and making us obsolete. It just hit me in that right zeitgeist, at that right little point."

"As a poor kid, there was no YouTube or cell phones, and we didn’t have computers," reminisces Leguizamo. "I used to go to the Broadcast Museum on 53rd Street and listen to old radio plays like The Shadow and these incredible detective radio plays. It's a different art form. With no visuals, your voice has to create the world. I thought that was an incredible challenge."

DeBose portrays the Wild Blue Yonder's confident First Officer Becca Bang, who’s stranded in a temporal mystery that might engulf her at any moment.

"I've yet to do anything like this, which is always exciting," she adds. "I was a little afraid of it, which told me I should do it. These gents are so talented. It's great company. It’s coming from brilliant minds who build worlds so impeccably. And it's about real stuff we’re dealing with today. I liked the idea that we could tell this story and make people listen and create a space for them to imagine themselves in it and see how they problem-solve to make the world a bit better."

Recording your character's lines is far more difficult than just stepping up to the microphone to read a script, and our ace "Exoplanet" trio delivered in every session.

"I just go in and throw myself at something," DeBose recalls. "I don’t really have a method. But I can tell you this: it is a full-body workout. I use everything at my disposal, whether it’s a chair or a pillow or running in place. I just do what the character does and end up sweating. And after three days, I have to go sit in silence. It's great. I love the idea of bringing back the radio play. The art of listening is such a thing. I don’t think people listen enough. Even for myself."

Likewise, Leguizamo embraced his booth sessions with exuberance and authenticity.

"You have to cancel the rest of your day, especially if you've got to talk, because your vocal chords are fried," he admits. "And if they're not fried you're not doing your job. You really have to do the physicality. If you run you have to run like a maniac and be out of breath. If I'm getting hit I start punching myself. Then there’s a sexiness to doing these things. Your voice has to have a little mystery, a little naughtiness. It’s an interesting intersection where you pull it back a little and invite the audience in.”

For Mackie, who’s used to athleticism needed to play MCU superheroes like The Falcon and Captain America, recording dialogue offered a different type of opportunity.

“I look for reasons not to talk to people, so I love doing these," he jokes. "Once I’m out of the studio, I’m not talking to anybody for two days. At a certain point for me, I find mentally I get tired of hearing myself talk. I just have to come home at cut off. I’ve said enough words for the next month.”

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

#703. Mary Hager, CBS News Politics and ‘Face the Nation’ Guru, to Retire

Mary Hager, the longtime political-news guru and behind-the-scenes force at CBS News and its Sunday public-affairs program, “Face the Nation,” will retire from the program in January, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Hager informed colleagues at CBS News of her decision on Wednesday, these people say, in order to give the Skydance news division time to search for a replacement. There is no obvious successor for Hager in her producer role at “Nation” at this time, largely because Anne Hsu, who was named the program’s executive producer in 2025, is moving to a new role within CBS News, according to the people familiar with the program. Related Stories 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs

CBS News declined to make executives available for comment. The media-industry newsletter Status previously reported on her decision. Hager could not be reached for immediate comment.

Hager is seen as a force at CBS News, and has been the guiding presence at “Face the Nation” during the tenures of moderators Bob Schieffer, John Dickerson and Margaret Brennan. She covered nearly every presidential campaign, convention and election night over the past 30 years at CBS News, in capacities that range from embed to anchor producer to executive producer of midterm coverage. She also spent more than 15 years as CBS News chief Washington correspondent Bob Schieffer’s producer.

And while she ran or helped run “Face The Nation” since 2011 as a senior producer, executive producer and senior executive producer, she also served in other capacities. Since 2022, she was also CBS News’ executive editor for politics.

In recent years, Hager placed emphasis on the quality of newsmaker bookings and discussions at “Nation,” in a belief that audiences were growing tired of some of the theatrics at the networks’ Sunday mainstays. “I think Sunday shows are getting further away from spin, and I think we are still doing a better job at kind of what we have always been trying to focus on — what is important for viewers, what the takeaways are, what they can learn, as opposed to putting the boxing gloves on and yelling back and forth,” she told Variety in 2019.

During the coronavirus pandemic, Hager helped transform the program into a reliable forum for medical information, dropping some of the political-news segments and turning instead to a medical expert, Scott Gottlieb, a former FDA commissioner. With Brennan on maternity leave for a few months, and John Dickerson filling in, “Nation” featured Gottlieb so many times that he became one of the most frequent non-journalist guests in the program’s history. At the time only Senator John McCain had been on “Nation” more times overall.

She will leave “Nation” as the show is faring well in the ratings. Season to date as of November 8, “Face The Nation” has won more viewers than either NBC’s “Meet The Press” or ABC’s “This Week.” And while it has lost some viewership compared to last season, the show has seen a surge among viewers between 26 and 54, the demographic coveted most by advertisers — and leads its rivals in that category as well.

Hager’s departure surfaces while the management of CBS News under a new owner, Skydance, has come under scrutiny. Since Skydance took over the company once known as Paramount and appointed Bari Weiss, a former digital entrepreneur and opinion journalist, as editor in chief, a number of prominent anchors and producers have chosen to exit. CBS News has also seen layoffs, with some staffers still mulling over buyout offers.

Hager’s retirement was said to be planned, according to people familiar with the matter, and not due to pressure or differences in vision. Even so, her absence from CBS News will be hard to fill in weeks to come.

#701. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

"Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," said LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study."

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected

When Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

But decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," said Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing."

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

Years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly important because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

Oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

The relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

Early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," said Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong."

The explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

When these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

"So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case."

This finding highlights an important distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

At the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," said Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production."

The research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

SpaceX is one big step closer to the 15th test flight of its Starship megarocket.

The company announced today (Nov. 10) that it had moved its latest Starship first stage, known as Super Heavy Booster 22, to the launch mount at its Starbase facility in South Texas ahead of Flight 15, which is scheduled to lift off this Friday (Nov. 13).

During the upcoming launch test, SpaceX plans to catch both Booster 22 and Starship's Ship upper stage with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms in a double landing catch — something the private spaceflight company has never tried before. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history.

Booster 22 therefore "was used for final catch testing upon arrival [at the pad], including a suspended squeeze test at catch height," SpaceX said in an X post today (Nov. 10).

That post shared four photos of the giant booster, which is powered by 33 of SpaceX's next-gen Raptor engines. The first shot showed Super Heavy in one of Starbase's "Mega Bay" assembly buildings before rollout, while the other three depicted it grasped by the tower's arms, held high in the South Texas sky.

SpaceX has used the chopstick arms during Starship flights before; it has successfully caught Super Heavy on three separate occasions. But the company has never attempted a catch of Ship, which flies higher and farther than the booster and is therefore a more challenging target. And SpaceX only reached orbit with Starship for the first time on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28.

So Flight 15 will break new ground. And, if all goes to plan, it will give us a look at the future: SpaceX plans to catch Super Heavy and Ship on all operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will allow the company to boost the megarocket's launch cadence.

And SpaceX wants to fly Starship incredibly often, so that it can build out its Starlink V3 broadband constellation and even bigger Starmind AI data-center network. Indeed, Elon Musk has said the company is eyeing 10,000 Starship flights per year by 2030.

If all goes to plan, Flight 15 will launch from Starbase on Friday during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time).

Super Heavy will return to Starbase for its catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff. Ship will follow suit much later — about 22 hours later, in fact, after it has deployed 26 Starlink V3 spacecraft into LEO and completed 14 circuits of our planet.

You can watch all the action live here at Space.com and get updates about the mission here.

Muniz, who picked up a second career as a racing driver in 2006, was scheduled to race as part of Team Air Force for Ford’s “Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic” event on Wednesday. #697. Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive

Mars may not be as geologically inactive as it appears. New evidence from mysterious gas emissions near an enormous Martian volcano suggests that heat and volcanic processes could still be present deep beneath the planet's surface.

Researchers have identified unusual concentrations of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures in the Alba Mons volcanic region. The findings suggest that gases from the planet's interior may be escaping through cracks in the surface, potentially revealing volcanic activity that has remained hidden until now.

An international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy believes the gas could originate from hot magma underground. If confirmed, this would indicate that Mars still has dormant volcanic systems capable of releasing gases to the surface.

The European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first detected hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in findings reported in 2021. On Earth, hydrogen chloride is frequently released through openings connected to magma, raising the possibility that similar processes could be occurring on Mars.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," says Daniel Mège, Professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the study published in Science Advances.

Mysterious Gas Emissions Defy Mars' Seasonal Pattern

The researchers noticed something unusual during early summer in the Martian northern hemisphere. Hydrogen chloride concentrations were unexpectedly elevated in a particular region, even though the gas normally becomes scarce at that time of year.

Hydrogen chloride levels on Mars generally follow a seasonal cycle. They typically peak during northern winter before declining to very low levels in summer. Scientists believe much of this behavior is associated with the planet's dust and water cycles.

However, the observations revealed a striking exception. Elevated hydrogen chloride repeatedly appeared in early summer over volcanic fractures on the slopes of Alba Mons. The unusual timing and consistent location suggested that something beyond ordinary atmospheric chemistry might be responsible.

Mars is home to the largest volcanoes in the Solar System, but scientists still do not know whether volcanic processes remain active beneath their surfaces.

Images taken from orbit indicate that some Martian volcanoes experienced eruptions within the past few million years. Instruments on the surface have also recorded marsquakes, demonstrating that the planet continues to experience seismic activity.

Together, these observations suggest that Mars may retain some of its geological energy. However, scientists have never directly observed a new volcanic eruption or fresh lava flow on the planet, leaving the question of present-day volcanism unresolved.

Fresh Cracks Reveal Clues to Hidden Volcanic Heat

To investigate the unusual gas concentrations, the research team combined atmospheric measurements with detailed observations of the Martian surface.

The Atmospheric Chemistry Suite aboard TGO uses infrared spectrometers to identify gases in the atmosphere. These instruments detected hydrogen chloride concentrated in a relatively small area shortly after the disappearance of winter frost.

Researchers then examined the same region using the orbiter's CaSSIS camera. The images revealed narrow fractures that appeared relatively fresh, with some extending hundreds of meters across the surface. Unusual changes in surface color were also visible around the cracks.

"The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," explains Daniel.

One possible explanation is that gases originating from magma deep underground travel upward through these fractures. On Earth, comparable volcanic openings are known as fumaroles.

The researchers propose that extremely cold Martian winters, when temperatures can fall to -120°C, allow ice to seal the fractures and temporarily prevent gases from escaping. As temperatures rise in early summer, the ice sublimates, changing directly into vapor and potentially opening pathways for underground gases to reach the atmosphere.

The discoloration observed around the fractures could also be significant. It may result from minerals or other substances deposited by escaping gases, similar to the deposits commonly found around fumaroles (volcanic gas vents) on Earth.

Although the connection between the gas emissions and volcanic fractures appeared promising, the researchers needed to rule out other explanations.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," concedes Daniel.

The team carefully evaluated the chemical reactions that could produce hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere, including processes unrelated to volcanism.

"A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food," adds Daniel.

After examining the atmospheric and geological evidence together, the researchers proposed that the gas could be escaping from a dormant magma chamber beneath Alba Mons. Such a chamber would form part of an underground volcanic system that could continue releasing gases even without producing visible eruptions.

Hidden Volcanic Activity Could Help Mars Support Life

The implications may extend beyond understanding the planet's geological history. Volcanic gases could also provide clues about how Mars evolved and whether it ever supported environments suitable for life.

In the distant past, gases released from magma, including hydrogen chloride, may have helped create a denser atmosphere and warmer conditions. Those conditions could have allowed liquid water to remain across large portions of the Martian surface.

Volcanic activity might also create habitable environments underground. If rising magma or lava comes into contact with groundwater, the interaction can produce warm hydrothermal systems. Such environments could provide both chemical energy and protection from the harsh conditions on the surface.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," ponders Daniel.

Although the findings do not establish that Mars is currently erupting or that life exists beneath its surface, they offer an intriguing new reason to investigate the volcanic fractures around Alba Mons.

"These findings may prove to be TGO's greatest success yet," highlights Colin Wilson, ESA's project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.
